chapter_summary:
Reaching the point where you can export and share your game is a significant milestone! It means you've taken an idea from concept, built core mechanics, added visuals and audio, and refined it through testing. Exporting your game, often referred to as "building" or "publishing," transforms your Unity project into a standalone application that can run on a target platform without needing the Unity editor. This process involves compiling all your code, assets, and scene data into a single package. Unity's "Build Settings" (File > Build Settings) is your primary interface for this. Here, you select your target platform (e.g., PC, Mac, Linux Standalone, WebGL, Android, iOS), ensuring you have the necessary build support modules installed for each. You'll also need to ensure all the scenes you want to be part of your game are listed in the "Scenes In Build" section. The order of scenes here matters, as the first scene in the list will be the one that loads when your game starts.

Beyond selecting the platform, configuring "Player Settings" (Edit > Project Settings > Player) is crucial for a polished release build. This is where you define your game's identity and how it presents itself to players. Under "Company Name" and "Product Name," you'll enter the official names. The "Icon" section allows you to set custom icons that will appear on the desktop or in app stores. The "Splash Image" section lets you customize the initial screen displayed when your game launches, often used for company logos or game titles. Under "Resolution and Presentation," you can set default screen resolution, fullscreen modes, and whether players can resize the window. For mobile platforms, you'll find settings for orientation (portrait/landscape) and specific API levels. For web builds (WebGL), you can configure loading bars and compression settings. Taking the time to properly fill out these settings gives your game a professional look and feel, even for a small project.

Before creating your final build, it's wise to consider some basic optimization. While advanced optimization is a deep topic, even simple steps can make a difference. Reducing the size of your textures (e.g., using smaller resolutions where appropriate, or setting proper compression in the Inspector) can significantly decrease build size and load times. Ensuring you're not loading unnecessary assets or running expensive calculations every frame can improve performance. For example, if an `AudioSource` or `Light` is not needed, disable or destroy it. If you have complex 3D models, consider reducing their polygon count. For 2D games, ensure your sprite packing is efficient. These small considerations contribute to a smoother experience for your players. A common mistake is to build the game without any optimization, leading to large file sizes, long load times, or poor frame rates, especially on less powerful machines.

Once your game is built, you'll have a folder containing an executable file (e.g., `.exe` for Windows, `.app` for Mac) and associated data folders. To share your game, you can simply zip this entire folder and distribute it. For Windows, players can extract the zip and run the `.exe` file. For Mac, they'll drag the `.app` bundle to their Applications folder. For WebGL builds, Unity generates an HTML file and a data folder, which can be hosted on a web server (or even locally opened in a browser, though some features might be restricted). Platforms like itch.io are excellent for sharing indie games and prototypes, offering easy upload and distribution. Remember to always provide clear instructions on how to install and run your game, along with any minimum system requirements. Sharing your game, no matter how small, is a fantastic achievement and a crucial step in getting your work out there and gathering real-world experience. It truly brings your game to life, allowing others to experience the world you've created.

screens.title: Exporting and Sharing Your Game
screens.subtitle: From Unity project to a shareable build — platform choices, Player Settings, and the final steps that make your game launch-ready.

narration.text: You’ve reached a major milestone: turning your playable prototype into a standalone application others can run. In this lesson you’ll learn what a build is, how Unity packages scenes and assets into a runnable program, and the essential Player Settings that give your game an identity — company and product names, icons, splash images, and resolution choices. You’ll also see basic optimization checks to reduce file size and improve performance before you press Build. As a concrete example, we’ll walk through preparing a Windows standalone build: verifying the scenes list, choosing the target platform, setting a product name and icon, and creating a folder for the final files. A common mistake is building without verifying scenes or leaving large uncompressed textures in the project; that leads to big downloads and long load times for players. By the end of this chapter you’ll know how to compile a build, test the executable outside the Editor, and package the build into a zip ready for sharing. Think about who will play your game and what device they’ll use, because platform choice shapes many of these decisions.

keyIdea.title: Transform your project into a runnable build
keyIdea.text: A build packages your scenes, assets, and code into a standalone application tailored to a target platform; preparing Player Settings and basic optimization makes that build professional and playable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Exporting and Sharing Your Game
Exporting and Sharing Your Game
What it means to build, configure, and share a release-ready game.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
This lesson shows a practical workflow: select a target platform, verify scenes in build, configure identity and presentation, run a test outside Unity, then package the build for distribution.
Why this matters
A polished build is how players first experience your game. Small details — icon, splash, resolution — influence first impressions and ease of installation.
In this lesson
How builds work and what to check before you build.
Coming up
Configure Player Settings to give your game identity.
Goal
Produce a runnable build and package it for sharing.
Build Preview
Visualizing the output folder and key files
Output Folder
A final build contains an executable and a data folder. Example: MyGame.exe and MyGame_Data. WebGL produces an index.html and data files.
MyGame_Final_Build/
MyGame.exe • MyGame_Data/ • README.txt
Distribution
Zip the full build folder before sharing. For web builds, host the generated files on a web server or a hosting platform that serves files over HTTP.
Tip: Include a short install/run instruction in a README to help players.
Key Takeaway

Building is the final packaging step. Confirm scenes, pick the right platform, set identity options, run a test build, and then package the folder for distribution.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter — skills that make your build release-ready.

narration.text: We’ll pause to make concrete commitments for this chapter. First, you will be able to build a standalone executable for a chosen platform, which means you know where to pick the platform and how to include the correct scenes. Second, you’ll configure essential Player Settings, such as company and product name, icon, splash image, and resolution options, so the game looks professional when it starts. Third, you will identify simple optimization opportunities — texture compression, unused assets, and reducing expensive per-frame operations — so builds are smaller and run smoother. Fourth, you’ll prepare a build folder and create a compressed zip that others can download and run. Each of these objectives is practical: they map to concrete steps in Unity’s menus and to common checks before you press Build. As you practice, notice common misconceptions: don’t assume the Editor’s play mode equals final performance, and don’t forget scene order in Build Settings. Achieving these objectives means your prototype becomes a shareable product players can run outside the Editor.

keyIdea.title: Goals for a release-ready build
keyIdea.text: Be able to select a platform, configure Player Settings, apply basic optimizations, and package the build for distribution.

screens.title: Objectives — Practical Steps and Reflection
screens.subtitle: Tasks and checks to complete during the build workflow and how to reflect on your release process.

narration.text: This continuation focuses on the hands-on steps and reflective skill you’ll practice. First, verify the Scenes In Build list and the order; the top scene is the first that runs, so confirm your main menu or initial level is placed first. Second, ensure you have the correct build support modules installed for your platform, because missing modules stop the build process. Third, test your new build outside Unity to confirm runtime behavior — this reveals differences in file paths, input handling, and performance. Fourth, practice writing short installation instructions and a minimum system requirements note to include with your distributed zip. These objectives map to concrete actions in Unity and to a habit of testing and documenting. A common misconception is that a successful Editor play session guarantees identical behavior in a built executable; running the build often uncovers platform-specific issues. Finishing these steps means you can not only create a build but also confidently hand it to players or testers.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on readiness and reflection
keyIdea.text: Confirm scenes, modules, and runtime behavior, then provide clear instructions so testers can run your build without friction.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Objectives — Practical Steps
Verify Scenes In Build
List every scene you want in the final game and arrange them so the first scene is your starting point. Missing or misordered scenes are a frequent cause of broken builds.
Checklist:
  • Open File → Build Settings
  • Ensure scenes are ticked and ordered
  • Save any open scenes before building
Confirm Build Support Modules
Make sure platform modules are installed so Unity can compile for that target. If a module is missing, the build dialog will prevent the build or fail partway through.
Test the Executable
Run the built executable on your machine to verify launch behavior, input, and performance. This uncovers issues not visible in the Editor.
Prepare Player Instructions
Include a short README with run instructions and minimum system requirements. Clear instructions reduce support questions and make playtests smoother.

screens.title: What is a Build?
screens.subtitle: Understand the compiled, standalone version of your game and why it differs from Editor play.

narration.text: A build is the compiled version of your Unity project that runs outside the Editor. It bundles scene data, assets, and compiled scripts into a package tailored for a target platform. Practically speaking, a Windows build produces an executable and a data folder, while WebGL produces an index. html and associated data files. The important distinction is that the Editor provides a runtime environment during development; a build must include everything your game needs to run on another machine. For example, a texture that loads in the Editor because it exists in the Assets folder may fail in a build if it was not referenced or included. One common misconception is that performance in the Editor is representative of the final build. Editor overhead, profiler attachments, and platform-specific graphics drivers mean real-world performance can differ. Concrete example: you may test in Editor at smooth frame rates and then find a lower FPS in the Windows executable due to different driver behavior or uncompressed textures. Key checks before building include verifying Scenes In Build, ensuring required assets are referenced, and confirming platform support modules are installed. Takeaway: treat a build as a real product — test it, document how to run it, and iterate based on player feedback.

keyIdea.title: Build = runnable product
keyIdea.text: A build packages code and assets so the game runs independently of the Editor; always test and verify assets and scenes before distributing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What is a Build?
Definition & core idea
A build compiles scenes, assets, and scripts into a standalone package for a specific platform. It must include every resource your game needs at runtime.
Example
Windows: MyGame.exe + MyGame_Data folder. WebGL: index.html + data files that must be served over HTTP.
Common mistake
Assuming Editor performance equals build performance. Always test the built executable to see real behavior.
Key takeaway
Treat the build as the product: verify scenes, referenced assets, and platform modules before distributing.
Quick checklist
  • Open File → Build Settings and confirm Scenes In Build
  • Select your Target Platform and ensure support modules are installed
  • Test the compiled executable on your machine
Reflection prompt
After your first build, what differences did you notice between Editor play and the executable? Use those observations to guide optimization and fixes.

screens.title: Using Build Settings and Scenes In Build
screens.subtitle: Select a target platform, add scenes, and set the startup order so your game launches correctly.

narration.text: Build Settings is the central workflow for creating a platform-specific build. Start by opening File → Build Settings, then choose the target platform such as PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, Android, iOS, or WebGL. A crucial step is adding the scenes you want distributed into the Scenes In Build list; only scenes present in this list are included. The first scene in the list becomes the initial scene when the executable launches, so place your main menu or splash scene at the top. A concrete walkthrough: save your open scenes, open Build Settings, click Add Open Scenes for each scene you want to include, drag to reorder so MainMenu is first, then select the target platform and press Switch Platform if needed. A common misconception is thinking all scenes in the Assets folder are included automatically — they are not. Also check that the appropriate platform support module is installed; if not, the build will not complete. When you press Build, Unity will ask for an output folder. Create a new folder like MyGame_Final_Build and select it. Unity will compile scripts, process assets, and write the executable and data files there. After the build finishes, open the folder and run the executable to validate startup and scene order. If the first scene is wrong or missing assets fail to load, return to the Editor to fix references and scene inclusion before rebuilding.

keyIdea.title: Scenes determine startup behavior
keyIdea.text: Only scenes listed in Build Settings are included in the build and the top-most scene is the launch scene — verify order and references before building.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Build Settings & Scenes
Step-by-step: Prepare Build Settings
  1. Save all open scenes in the Editor to prevent lost changes.
  2. Open File → Build Settings and choose the target platform.
  3. Use Add Open Scenes to include each scene you want in the build.
  4. Drag scenes to order them; the first scene is the startup scene.
  5. If needed, click Switch Platform to enable the correct build support.
  6. Click Build and choose a new output folder for the final files.
Example folder name
MyGame_Final_Build — contains the executable and a data folder.
Quick reference
// Build Settings checklist (notes for your README)
1. Ensure MainMenu scene is first
2. Verify all referenced assets are in included scenes
3. Switch Platform if target differs from current
4. Build to a new, clearly named folder
5. Test executable after build
Misconception
Assets in the Project folder are not automatically included — only assets referenced by included scenes and resources are packaged.

screens.title: Configuring Player Settings
screens.subtitle: Give your game identity and presentation: company/product name, icon, splash image, and resolution options.

narration.text: Player Settings is where you define how your game presents itself. Company Name and Product Name set the metadata visible in install locations and system dialogs. The Icon section lets you assign images that appear on the desktop, taskbar, or app store listings; for Windows, icons often require a. ico file and for other platforms you can use. png variants. The Splash Image controls the initial screen players see when your game launches — use it to display a studio logo or title card. Under Resolution and Presentation you decide default screen sizes, fullscreen behavior, and whether the player can resize the window. For mobile builds, orientation and A P I-level options are available. A practical example: set Product Name to your game title, assign a 512x512 PNG for high-resolution stores, and choose Fullscreen Window for a polished PC experience. A mistake to avoid is leaving placeholder names or missing icons, which makes your build feel unpolished. Another trap is enabling resizable windows without adapting UI layouts, which can break HUD placement. After updating Player Settings, rebuild and test to confirm the icon, splash, and resolution behave as expected across your target platforms. Final question to reflect on: which presentation choices will give the best first impression for your players and why?

keyIdea.title: Player Settings define presentation
keyIdea.text: Filling out identity, icon, splash, and presentation settings gives your build a professional first impression and predictable runtime behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Player Settings
Identity fields
Company Name and Product Name become metadata in the built application and stores. Use consistent, final values before release to avoid confusing players or reviewers.
Icon guidance
Provide appropriately sized images for target platforms. Windows commonly needs .ico; other platforms accept PNGs with multiple resolutions.
Splash and Presentation
Customize the splash screen or choose to disable Unity splash if your license allows. Configure default resolution, fullscreen mode, and window resizability to match your design goals.
Practical tip
If your UI is not responsive, avoid enabling resizable windows. For mobile, lock orientation to portrait or landscape depending on your gameplay.

screens.title: Basic Optimization Checks Before Building
screens.subtitle: Quick, high-impact steps to reduce build size and avoid runtime slowdowns.

narration.text: Before you create a final build, run a short optimization checklist. These are small changes that often produce large benefits. First, audit textures: reduce resolution for textures that are never viewed full-screen and enable platform-appropriate compression in the Inspector. This directly lowers build size and memory usage. Second, remove or disable unused assets and scenes; unused prefabs, audio files, or art assets included in the project can inflate the build if referenced. Third, check expensive per-frame operations: avoid heavy computations in Update unless necessary; move physics or interval checks to FixedUpdate or coroutines where appropriate. Fourth, disable or remove AudioSource or Light components not needed at runtime to reduce processing. For complex 3D models, consider reducing polygon counts or using LODs; for 2D projects, ensure efficient sprite packing. A concrete example: change a 4096x4096 UI texture to 1024x1024 and enable compression — build size can drop significantly with minimal visual loss. Common misconception: optimization equals removing quality; instead, it’s about matching asset fidelity to actual on-screen needs. After each change, rebuild and test the executable to confirm that performance and visuals meet expectations. This iterative approach helps you find the sweet spot between polish and performance before you share your game.

keyIdea.title: Small optimizations, big impact
keyIdea.text: Texture size, unused assets, and unnecessary per-frame work are common levers to reduce build size and improve runtime performance.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Basic Optimization Checks
Quick optimization checklist
  • Texture audit: resize and enable compression where appropriate.
  • Remove unused assets or scenes and clear references to them.
  • Disable unnecessary AudioSource and Light components.
  • Move heavy per-frame calculations out of Update when possible.
  • Use sprite packing for 2D projects and LODs for 3D models.
Concrete example
A single high-resolution texture can dominate build size. Reducing a 4096 texture to 1024 and compressing it often yields big savings with little visible change in gameplay contexts.
Pro tip
Iterate: make one optimization, rebuild, and compare build size and runtime behavior to validate benefits.
Don't do this
Avoid global deletion without backups. Keep a clean branch or a copy of the project before large asset removals.

screens.title: Platform Differences: Desktop, Mobile, and WebGL
screens.subtitle: How target platform choices change Player Settings, presentation, and distribution steps.

narration.text: Choosing a target platform affects both build steps and runtime expectations. Desktop builds (Windows, Mac, Linux) produce executables and data folders; you typically set window behavior, fullscreen mode, and icons. Mobile builds require attention to orientation, A P I levels, and touch input; icons and splash screens must meet store guidelines. WebGL builds generate H T M L and data files that must be served over HTTP; opening files directly from disk may fail due to browser security restrictions. A concrete contrast: when building for WebGL you’ll configure compression and a loading bar because browsers stream assets differently, and you must host the output on a web server. For mobile, you might lock orientation to portrait and test memory usage carefully because mobile devices are often less powerful. A common mistake is treating one set of Player Settings as universal; for instance, windowed mode settings are irrelevant for mobile. Another misconception is that any build will run identically across devices — platform-specific drivers, permissions, and input methods always require testing on the actual platform. Practical workflow: pick a primary target, adjust Player Settings for that target, perform a build, test on the target device or environment, and iterate. This targeted testing reduces surprises and ensures your final distribution matches player expectations.

keyIdea.title: Platform choice changes everything
keyIdea.text: Desktop, mobile, and WebGL builds have distinct Player Settings, runtime behavior, and distribution methods — always test on the target environment.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Platform Differences
Desktop (Windows/Mac/Linux)
Produces an executable and data folder. Configure icons, fullscreen mode, and window resizability. Test installers or simple run instructions.
Mobile (Android/iOS)
Pay attention to orientation, API levels, touch input, and store icon requirements. Test on real devices for performance and memory behavior.
WebGL
Generates HTML and data files that need a web server to run properly. Configure compression and loading behavior for web delivery.
Practical checklist
  • Choose the primary target and install its build support module.
  • Adjust Player Settings to match platform expectations.
  • Build and test in the target environment (desktop executable, mobile device, or web server).

screens.title: What a Build Produces — Files and Folders
screens.subtitle: Understand the executable, data folder, and the files you will distribute

narration.text: When Unity finishes a build it produces a packaged application specific to the chosen platform. The important idea is that a build is more than a single file: it is an executable plus supporting data. For a Windows standalone you'll typically see an executable such as MyGame dot exe and an associated MyGame_Data folder containing textures, scene data, and runtime resources. Mac builds are packaged as an application bundle and often appear as a single app file that users move into Applications. WebGL builds generate an index dot html file and one or more data files that the browser loads. This structure matters because if any supporting file is missing the executable will fail to run or will crash at runtime. A common mistake is to copy only the executable and forget the data folder. Another gotcha is modifying files inside the data folder after the build; those files are generated to match the executable and should remain intact. As a quick check, after building, open the output folder, inspect the executable and the data folder, and confirm a reasonable file size and timestamps. That simple inspection often saves hours of debugging. Ask yourself: do I have everything needed to run this package on another machine?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: A build is an executable plus one or more data folders; always distribute the whole output folder so resources and scenes load correctly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Build Output
What you get
A platform-specific executable and the supporting data folder that contains assets, scene data and runtime files. This pair must travel together when sharing your build.
  • Executable file (Windows: dot exe, Mac: app bundle)
  • Data folder with scenes, textures, and assets
  • Platform-specific runtime files and metadata
Quick example
Windows build folder contents:
MyGame.exe
MyGame_Data/
  managed/
  resources.assets
  sharedassets0.assets
Key Takeaway

Always keep the executable and its entire data folder together when distributing. If a file is missing the build may not start or will break at runtime.

Build Output Preview
Example: Windows standalone
Folder tree
MyGame_Final_Build/
MyGame.exe
MyGame_Data/
managed/
resources.assets
sharedassets0.assets
Checks to run
  • Confirm executable exists and is recent.
  • Confirm data folder is present and non-empty.
  • Verify file sizes look reasonable (not zero bytes).
  • Do not edit files generated by Unity inside the data folder.
Common Mistake
Copying only the executable to share and omitting the data folder. The program will fail to load scenes or assets.

screens.title: Testing Your Built Game Outside the Editor
screens.subtitle: How to run, verify features, and catch runtime problems before sharing

narration.text: Running and testing your game outside the Unity editor is a vital final step. A build may behave differently than Play mode, so testing confirms player input, scene loading, resolution, audio, and performance on a target machine. Start by launching the executable in the build folder and walk through core flows you expect players to use: main menu, first level, UI, and exit. Verify that your first scene loads as intended — remember, Unity uses the first scene listed in Scenes In Build as the startup scene. Check that icons and splash screens display according to your Player Settings and that resolution and fullscreen behave as expected. If something is missing, look for absent assets in the data folder or errors in the game's log files. If audio or textures fail to appear, confirm those assets were included in the build and not excluded by platform-specific settings. A common misconception is assuming the editor is an exact replica of a final build; it is not. Differences in file access, compression, and runtime platform code can reveal bugs only visible in a standalone build. After testing, note bugs, reproduce them consistently, and fix them in the project before rebuilding. How would you reproduce a visual bug reliably on another machine?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Always run the built executable on a target machine and verify key player flows and assets; editor success does not guarantee a clean release.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Release Testing
Testing Checklist
  1. Launch the executable and confirm the startup scene loads.
  2. Play through main menu, at least one level, and exit flows.
  3. Verify icons and splash appear per Player Settings.
  4. Check resolution, fullscreen, and input responsiveness.
  5. Inspect build folder logs for errors if available.
Pro Tip
Document any reproduction steps and the exact build folder contents before sharing with testers. This speeds debugging and helps isolate platform-specific issues.
Example scenario
You launch MyGame dot exe and notice the title screen appears but no background music plays. You check the data folder to confirm the audio asset exists then run the build on a second machine to verify whether this is machine-specific or a missing asset in the build.
Debugging Hints
If a feature fails, reproduce it, note exact steps, and inspect the build output folder for missing assets. Keep a short reproduction guide to share with collaborators.
// Example local test log excerpt (illustrative)
[INFO] Game started
[INFO] Loaded scene: MainMenu
[WARN] Missing audio clip: bg_music
[ERROR] Failed to load resource: resources.assets
Misconception
Passing Play mode tests guarantees a flawless build. In reality, platform differences and packaging can reveal different failures.

screens.title: Preparing and Zipping Your Build for Sharing
screens.subtitle: A practical, hands-on packaging workflow you can follow now

narration.text: Packaging your build into a single archive makes sharing simple and protects files from accidental omission. The essential rule is: zip the entire build folder, not just individual files. For a Windows standalone create a new folder named MyGame_Final_Build on your desktop, then instruct Unity to build into that folder. After the build completes, verify the executable and the data folder are both inside. On Windows, right-click the MyGame_Final_Build folder and choose Send to then Compressed (zipped) folder. On Mac, right-click and choose Compress MyGame_Final_Build. The result is a MyGame_Final_Build dot zip file that contains everything a player needs. When you share this zip file with testers, include a short README that explains how to extract the zip and how to run the executable (for example, double-click MyGame dot exe on Windows). A frequent error is zipping only the executable or forgetting the README and minimum system requirements. Good packaging also protects platform-specific metadata and simplifies uploads to distribution platforms. After zipping, test the zip by extracting it to a clean folder and running the game to ensure nothing was missed.

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Zip the full build folder and include a README with run instructions; test the extracted package on a clean machine before sharing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Zipping & Packaging
Step-by-step
  1. Build into a new, empty folder named MyGame_Final_Build.
  2. Verify MyGame dot exe and MyGame_Data are inside the folder.
  3. Right-click the folder and choose Compress/Send to Compressed (zipped) folder.
  4. Add a README with run instructions and minimum system requirements.
  5. Test extraction and run the game on another machine.
Example README
1. Extract MyGame_Final_Build dot zip. 2. On Windows double-click MyGame dot exe. 3. Minimum: Windows 10, 4GB RAM, GPU with drivers installed.
Visual checklist
[ ] Executable present
[ ] Data folder present and non-empty
[ ] README included with extraction instructions
[ ] Zip tested by extracting to another folder
Common Mistake
Zipping only the executable instead of the full folder causes missing assets and runtime failures for players who extract and run the game.

screens.title: Hosting WebGL and Sharing on Platforms
screens.subtitle: Why WebGL needs a server and practical distribution options like itch dot io

narration.text: WebGL builds differ from desktop builds because they rely on the browser to load data files via HTTP. A crucial point is that most browsers block local file access for security reasons, so opening index dot html directly from the file system often fails. This is why WebGL builds require hosting on a web server, even a small local one, to function correctly. You can run a simple local server to test a WebGL build, or upload the zipped WebGL output to a hosting service. Distribution platforms such as itch dot io are a user-friendly way to share desktop builds and WebGL projects. They accept uploaded zips and provide a player and download mechanics for users. When preparing a WebGL upload, include the index dot html and all generated data and code files in the package. For desktop builds, upload the zipped folder and provide extraction and run instructions in the project description. A common error is sharing WebGL files without telling testers to host them or uploading only index dot html without the data folder. When you share, always include minimum system requirements and any special instructions to reduce user confusion. How will you instruct your players to run your build?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: WebGL builds must be served over HTTP; use a local server for testing or upload the full build to a hosting platform like itch dot io for easy sharing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Hosting & Platforms
Why WebGL needs a server
Browsers restrict local file access for security. WebGL builds load additional data files via HTTP, so they must be served by a web server. Testing locally without a server often causes load errors and corrupt data requests.
What to upload
  • Include index dot html and all related data and code files generated by WebGL build.
  • Zip the full WebGL output for upload if required by the host.
  • Provide run instructions and any known browser recommendations.
Platform notes
itch dot io — Easy indie-focused distribution. Upload a zip, add a description, and share a link with players.
Direct hosting — Use any web server to host your WebGL folder; testers open the URL to play.
Common Mistake
Sharing index dot html alone or asking testers to open it locally. Always package the full output and instruct testers to host or extract it correctly.

screens.title: Final Release Checklist & Common Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: A compact checklist to run through before you publish

narration.text: Before you publish, run a concise release checklist to avoid easy mistakes. First, confirm your Scenes In Build list contains the scenes you intend, with the correct first scene set to load at startup. Second, review Player Settings: company and product names, icon, splash image, resolution defaults, and platform-specific options like orientation for mobile. Third, do a basic optimization pass: reduce texture sizes where possible, remove unused assets, and disable unnecessary runtime components. Fourth, create the build and test it thoroughly on a target machine, verifying menus, audio, input, and performance. Fifth, prepare packaging: include a README with run instructions and minimum requirements, zip the entire build folder, and test extracting and running from the zip. Sixth, choose an appropriate distribution channel and upload the full package. Common pitfalls include building without verifying scenes in build, forgetting to include the data folder, and skipping a local extraction test. A final practical habit is to keep a versioned naming scheme for builds, for example MyGame_v1 dot 0_Final, so you and your testers know which build they are testing. Which checklist item will you add to your next release?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: A short, repeatable checklist prevents common release errors: confirm scenes, finalize player settings, optimize, test the build, and package everything with clear instructions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Release Checklist
Final Release Checklist
Scene & Build
Verify Scenes In Build order and first scene startup.
Player Settings
Confirm company name, product name, icons, splash image, and resolution settings.
Optimization
Compress textures, remove unused assets, and simplify models where appropriate.
Test Run
Run the executable, play core flows, and check for missing assets or crashes.
Package
Zip the full build folder, include README and minimum requirements, and test extraction.
Distribute
Choose a host, upload the package, and provide clear player instructions.
Common Pitfall
Skipping a full extraction and run test. Always extract the zip to a clean folder and run the included executable to confirm nothing was left out.
Why this matters
These steps protect your players from installation confusion and reduce the time you spend troubleshooting distribution problems.

narration.text: Here are six compact concepts you should retain as you prepare and share your game. First, a Build is the compiled, standalone version of your game that includes an executable and its supporting data; treating the build as a single package prevents missing files. Second, Player Settings define the game's identity—company and product names, icons, splash images, and resolution options—and these settings shape player first impressions. Third, Target Platform refers to the operating system or device you build for; each platform produces different output files and may require separate testing. Fourth, Optimization is the set of practices to reduce build size and improve runtime performance, like sensible texture sizes and avoiding unnecessary runtime calculations. Fifth, WebGL is a web build target that produces an index dot html plus data files and must be served over HTTP to work in modern browsers. Sixth, Distribution describes how you share the package, whether by zipping and sending directly or uploading to a platform such as itch dot io. Keep these terms in mind as short reminders when you finalize and share your project.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Remember the build is a package; finalize Player Settings, optimize assets, test on target platforms, and choose a distribution method that fits your audience.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts
Build
The compiled, runnable package that includes the executable and required data files for the platform.
Player Settings
Global build properties such as company name, product name, icon, splash image, and resolution settings.
Target Platform
The OS or device you build for; determines output format and may need separate testing and settings.
Takeaway: Keep a short checklist for each concept and run it before packaging your final build.

narration.text: A few more short reminders will help you avoid last-minute problems. Optimization reduces build size and improves runtime performance; even small changes like compressing textures or removing unused assets can make load times shorter. WebGL requires proper hosting because browsers block local file access; always test WebGL builds on a web server or upload to a hosting service. Distribution is the process of getting your build to players — zipping the full build folder and including a README simplifies the experience. When sharing, include minimum system requirements and extraction instructions to avoid support requests about missing files. Finally, always test the extracted zip on a clean machine to ensure the package runs independent of your development environment. These practical steps reduce friction for your players and free you to focus on polishing gameplay. Which of these steps will you prioritize before your next share?

keyIdea.title: Final Reminder
keyIdea.text: Small optimizations, clear packaging, and platform-aware hosting make your game easier to play and test — do them before you share.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts (cont.)
Optimization
Reduce textures, remove unnecessary assets, and avoid expensive per-frame calculations to improve player experience.
WebGL Hosting
Must be served over HTTP. Local file access often blocks data loads. Use a simple server or a hosting platform for reliable playback.
Distribution
Zip the full build, include instructions and requirements, and test extraction before uploading to your chosen platform.
Takeaway: tidy packaging and clear instructions save time for you and your players. Test everything one last time before sharing.
